On April 17 the member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) asked a question as to when the Bankruptcy Act, 1949, would be proclaimed. At that time I said the matter was under consideration with the new superintendent of bankruptcy, and that an announcement would be made in due course. I should like to make that announcement now.
The Bankruptcy Act, 1949, received royal assent on December 10, 1949. Since that time the bankruptcy branch of the Department of Justice has been engaged in the preparation of a draft of general rules to be made by the governor in council under the act. This draft consists of a large number of rules, tariff items and forms. All the official receivers and registrars in bankruptcy were asked in December, 1949, for their comments and suggestions in connection with this draft, and replies are still being received from them. On April 13 last copies of this draft were sent to certain bankruptcy court judges and officials who were requested to let the superintendent of bankruptcy have their comments before May 1 next.
Various interested parties and organizations have made representations concerning these rules, which have raised questions of policy which will have to be settled before the final form of the rules is decided upon. When the general rules have been settled and have been passed by the governor in council, we propose to have them printed and distributed to all the trustees and to officials of the bankruptcy courts in sufficient time for these officials to familiarize themselves with the act and the rules before the act is proclaimed.
At the present time we consider that the earliest date on which it would be appropriate to proclaim the Bankruptcy Act, 1949, would be July 1, 1950.
REGULATIONS TO IMPLEMENT KELLOCK REPORT ON "noronic" DISASTER

On December 8 last, Mr. Speaker, I indicated to the house that the recommendations of the commissioner in the investigation

Steamship Inspection
of the Noronic disaster would be incorporated in the regulations of the steamship inspection service of the Department of Transport. On my instructions, departmental officers immediately applied themselves to this task, and late in December proposed regulations incorporating the recommendations of the commissioner were circulated to all ship owners to whom the new regulations would apply. Since the beginning of the year the steamship inspection board has had occasion to meet with representatives of the industry, not only in Ottawa but also on the Pacific coast.
It is the right of the public to demand reasonable protection when travelling by ship, and after most serious consideration, and on the advice of the board of steamship inspection and other officers of my department, it was decided to use the international convention for the safety of life at sea as a guide in the preparation of regulations to implement the Kellock report.
The convention to which I refer was held in London in 1948. It was composed of technical experts of almost all the maritime nations of the world, and I am sure no recognized authority would assert that the provisions of this convention do not afford the protection to which the public is entitled.
The recommendations made by the commissioner are to be implemented as far as conditions will permit. On existing ships the period of time between now and the placing of these ships in commission is too short to allow complete compliance with all the regulations; however, the principal requirements will be implemented and as 'many of the others as time will permit. No passenger ship will be allowed to enter into service without complying with the new regulations to the extent which is practicable.
Several ship owners have already taken steps to implement many of the commissioner's recommendations. One firm on the Pacific coast has had fire-resisting bulkheads and several other additional items of equipment fitted in one of its ships, and arrangements are being made for similar changes on another of their vessels. An eastern company operating on the St. Lawrence river and great lakes has arranged, before placing four of its ships in commission this summer, to have fire-resisting bulkheads, a partial sprinkling system, public address system, fire detection system, fire alarm system and manually supervised patrol system fitted throughout each of its four ships.
In the application of the regulations, care will be taken to avoid the necessity of curtailment of services. Decisions in these matters

will, consistent with safety, be made by the board of steamship inspection and not by any individual steamship inspector.
In all forms of passenger transportation, be it by air, rail, or water, there is always, of course, an element of hazard, and conditions are and will continue to be frequently reviewed in order to limit these hazards as much as possible. I am satisfied that passengers on board Canadian ships will be receiving a much greater amount of protection under the new regulations. These have been approved by order in council P.C, 1896, of April 12, 1950, copy of which I now table.

Will new regulations be introduced at this session pertaining to small craft driven by gasoline or diesel motive power? I refer to craft under sixty-five feet in length.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: OUTBREAK OF NEWCASTLE DISEASE IN BRITISH COLUMBIA FLOCKS
speechtext:
I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Agriculture. In view of the report of the outbreak of a dread disease, known as Newcastle disease, among poultry flocks in British Columbia, would the minister care to make a statement?
Inquiries of the Ministry

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: OUTBREAK OF NEWCASTLE DISEASE IN BRITISH COLUMBIA FLOCKS
speechtext:
The hon. member was kind enough to give me notice of his question, and I have a short prepared statement with regard to the matter.
In regard to Newcastle disease in poultry, there has been an outbreak of Newcastle disease in a number of poultry flocks in the Fraser valley area of British Columbia. The first case was discovered and dealt with on February 26, 1950. Up to April 19 the disease has been reported and dealt with in seventeen additional flocks. The total number of birds involved to date is approximately 45,000. This is out of an estimated population of 3 million birds in British Columbia.
Since Newcastle disease in poultry is highly infectious and the mortality rate is heavy, it is extremely important that action be taken to prevent its establishment and spread throughout the poultry flocks of Canada. For some years past there have been occasional outbreaks in different provinces, and all have been dealt with in the same way, namely, by quarantine, slaughter, disinfection of premises, and compensation to the owners for the birds slaughtered. This method has kept the disease from gaining a foothold in Canada and has protected the poultry industry generally against heavy losses which almost certainly would have followed the uncontrolled spread of the disease.
With regard to the British Columbia outbreak, the indications are that new cases are diminishing in number and importance. Dr. Kenneth Wells, of the headquarters staff of the health of animals division, has flown to Vancouver to make an on-the-spot check of the situation and to keep us fully informed. He will also confer with provincial authorities as to what is being done, and what, if any, additional action might be taken.
It has been suggested by several people that we should abandon our present slaughter and compensation policy and instead authorize the importation and use of vaccine. So far departmental officials believe that a vaccination policy would be unwise, even though the efficacy of vaccine were proven, about which there is some doubt. It is pointed out that once the present policy of rigid control is abandoned, all poultry flock owners might be faced with the alternative of vaccination or the acceptance of heavy losses from the disease itself. While there is every hope of keeping complete control of the situation by the present methods, it seems highly inadvisable to subject the entire industry to the risk and expense which would

Inquiries of the Ministry be involved in the substitution of a vaccination policy. The departmental officers will continue to watch the situation closely and report frequently on developments.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. E. Harris (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a brief review of the work of the department, but before doing so I should like to thank all those hon. members who in the past three or four months have been kind enough to express to me personally and in the house their good wishes on my appointment to this office. I hope they will continue to show their good will by severely criticizing any shortcomings there may be in the estimates this afternoon.
In view of the announcement on many occasions that amendments to the Indian Act will be introduced at this session, I do not propose to deal at great length with the Indian affairs branch of the department. I am prepared, however, to give some figures with respect to education and other matters mentioned in the discussion of the estimates last fall, if it is so desired. I should like, though, to say something in particular about the immigration and citizenship branches.
Although the coming into being of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration dates only from January of this year, its main branches have roots in early Canadian history. There is continuity of Indian affairs administration for about two hundred years. Citizenship registration-or naturalization as it was formerly known-and immigration go back to confederation.
The organization of the new department has not resulted in any substantial increase in personnel. A departmental administration branch became necessary and has been partly established. A construction unit had to be added to the Indian affairs branch, to take over Indian affairs engineering and construction works. Personnel for both units has

been secured from the former departments of mines and resources and reconstruction and supply.
The Prime Minister stated in the house on November 26 last:
Having citizenship, immigration and Indian affairs in the one department would indicate that the purpose of the activities of that department was to make Canadian citizens of those who were horn here of the original inhabitants of the territory, or those who migrated to this country.
The aim of the immigration branch of the department is to promote an increase in the population of Canada of carefully selected, readily assimilable immigrants within the absorptive capacity of the country. The aim of the citizenship branch is to bring about full understanding and acceptance by such persons and by the Indian population as well of the benefits and responsibilities of Canadian citizenship. It is not claimed that the objective is new-simply that it is being accentuated and the work co-ordinated.
There have been several significant migrations to Canada: the initial French settlement; the movement of British Empire Loyalists; migration from the British isles in the 1830's, and the general settlement of the west fifty years ago.
Shortly before the turn of the century the Canadian government instituted a vigorous immigration policy, with free or low-cost homesteads being held out as an inducement to land settlers. During the years 1901-1915 Canada received 2,920,625 immigrants- approximately 40 per cent from the British isles and over 30 per cent from the United States.
World war I brought to an end the heavy land settlement era, and immigration remained at a comparatively low ebb from then until 1927, when there was an upswing which lasted until 1930. Solicitation of immigration from any country was discontinued at this time, and the admissible classes narrowed. There was no substantial increase up to 1939, when the second world war intervened.
During the calendar year period 1945-49, 379,199 persons were admitted to Canada, of whom 173,090 came from the British isles and 42,428 from the United States.
Perhaps the refugee movement calls for special mention. Canada was one of the first countries to assist the United Nations in the resettlement of the millions of persons displaced from their native countries as a result of world war II. This movement has been co-ordinated by the immigration branch with the full co-operation of the departments of labour and national health and welfare. To date. 98,000 refugees have been admitted to

Applications for admission of groups of skilled and unskilled workers have been made by industries and screened by an interdepartmental committee consisting of representatives of the immigration branch and the departments of labour, external affairs and national health and welfare. Under the group movement plan, approval has been given to the admission of refugees for such employment as miners, railway workers, hydro construction workers, domestics, clothing industry workers, et cetera.
The selection, processing, transportation and reception in Canada of refugees are carried out in co-operation with the international refugee organization and the Canadian Christian council for resettlement of refugees and the departments mentioned.
The international refugee organization estimates that on June 30 next there will be approximately 405,600 coming within its mandate in camps in Europe. Of these, 216,000 are considered to be suitable for resettlement somewhere. At the present time Canada is accepting domestics and farm workers from these camps. IRO care of refugees was to have ceased on June 30, but is being continued until March 31, 1951.
Getting back to the general question, in May, 1947, Mr. King, as prime minister, outlined to the house government policy in the matter of immigration. He said:
The policy of the government is to foster the growth of the population of Canada by the encouragement of immigration. The government will seek by legislation, regulation and vigorous administration to ensure the careful selection and permanent settlement of such numbers of immigrants as can advantageously be absorbed in the national economy.
Mr. King also indicated that it was not proposed to alter the immigration regulations in a manner that might bring about any fundamental change in the character of the population.
The basic races of Canada are French and Anglo-Saxon. W-ith respect to immigration from France, it is regrettable that only 3,404 immigrants came to Canada from that country since the end of the war. France has not encouraged emigration for some time, and having suffered great losses in manpower in two wars within a generation, she is seeking immigration to augment her own manpower requirements. Monetary restrictions and the traditional attitude of the French towards emigration also contribute to the small movement to this country.
Is that a government agency?

Yes.
The foundation arranges transportation, which is paid for by the emigrant. In Canada the movement is handled by a nomination method under which applications are made for Netherlands farmers by Canadian farmers. Settlement arrangements are investigated by the settlement service of the immigration branch.
The movement of these Netherlands agriculturists is working out very satisfactorily. About 3,000 came during 1947, 7,000 during 1948, 7,000 during 1949, and about 1,500 to date in 1950.
With few exceptions the encouragement of immigration to Canada has public support. I think we all agree that this country has benefited from past immigration. I think we all agree that this country can support a much larger population. The extent of our export trade, the tremendous production of foodstuffs, and our great natural resources, all lead to this conclusion.
Immigration policy requires the support of all Canadians, and generally speaking that support has been given. There has always been a view, though it is not widely held in Canada, that immigration may add to unemployment. There is the opposite view that immigration aids employment, and at one time or another I suppose an argument can be made out for each side. However, the statistics of unemployment during the past winter and the known destination of the immigrants would seem to indicate that employment has been aided by immigration. For example, in the province of Ontario, which received the largest number of immigrants, 183,000, out of a total of 379,000, employment was highest this winter with respect to both the total population and the total working force. Nevertheless I do not propose to argue this point, as the policy which has already been stated recognizes that from time to time the numbers to be admitted to this country would vary, having in mind conditions here.
In many instances immigrants have brought about increased opportunities for employment by Canadians through the introduction of new skills and techniques.
A good example is the so-called "refugee industries". A recent memorandum of the dominion bureau of statistics shows that 72 industries established by immigrants between 1939 and 1947 employed at the end of that year 6,127 workers to whom they paid, in that single year, $11,228,293 in salaries and wages. The gross value of the products of these industries for 1947 was $50,720,126. The

aggregate figure of salaries and wages paid by "refugee industries'' between 1939 and 1947 is $62,797,422, and the global gross value of their products, $264,249,063.
To this most impressive contribution to the national economy, which has resulted directly from immigration, must be added the very large amount of capital brought to Canada by immigrants. Between September 1, 1945, and December 31, 1949, immigrants brought or transferred to Canada funds estimated by the Bank of Canada at $168 million. The value of what is known as settlers' effects, the personal belongings of immigrants, brought into the country during the same period amounted to $48 million.
It will be seen that some of the factors involved in immigration are the opportunities for the immigrant in Canada for land settlement or employment and the obtaining of the most desirable immigrants from abroad who can settle on the land or take the available employment. There are difficulties of exchange at the moment, and whether this can be overcome or not I am not prepared to say at this time; but the house can be assured that we shall adhere to the policy previously enunciated, having in mind the high quality of our citizens and the desirability of maintaining that high standard. We need both capital and people to aid in the development of our resources, and we believe that we are pursuing the best course to further this policy.
My remarks have related solely to immigration, but the reception of visitors to Canada represents a substantial portion of the duties of the immigration branch. Approximately 40 million people were checked into Canada during 1949, including the 95,000 immigrants. In order to facilitate the entry of tourists, other visitors, returning Canadians and commuters, two hundred and eighty ports of entry are operated by this department and require a staff, including part-time employees, of 1,728.
It will, therefore, be seen that the immigration branch has to maintain personnel and offices capable of receiving into Canada every year approximately 40 million people, of which only roughly one in 400 is an immigrant seeking permanent landing. Of the remainder, 24 million are tourists, and we of course are happy to have these people come to see our country and its opportunities, as no doubt we do obtain not only permanent business contacts but probably some permanent settlers out of this number. The remainder of the 40 million are Canadians who go abroad on business or as visitors, and for whom we have to provide the facilities of re-entry, or are commuters living in Canada

It is part of our economy that these people should be free to work at American border points and go and come daily earning their livelihood in this manner; but it should be remembered that, in order to permit this to be done, quite substantial immigration facilities have to be provided at a considerable cost.
The Canadian Citizenship Act became effective on January 1, 1947, and the administration of this act is the responsibility of the Canadian citizenship registration branch. This is a continuation of the work handled by the old naturalization branch of the Department of the Secretary of State.
There was a great increase in the work during 1947 and 1948, and the volume of applications for citizenship remained at the higher level. I should like to have consent to place on Hansard a statement of the certificates granted and revoked since the act came in force.

The Canadian citizenship branch is a division separate from the Canadian citizenship registration branch, and is designed to assist immigrants and others who are applicants for citizenship in receiving instructions in the responsibilities and privileges of Canadian citizenship.
We believe that every applicant for citizenship should share a deep conviction of the worth of the individual and the principles of democracy as we know them; we believe that there should be a greater consciousness amongst our people of the achievements of the Canadian nation, and that we should do our utmost to promote Canadian unity so that all of our people may embrace one steadfast purpose-to be good Canadian citizens.

We believe that our Canadian system is based on service to all the persons who comprise the state, and that we desire only the welfare of our people. There is no such thing as the welfare of the state as such, but only the collective welfare of all the families and individuals within our borders. Certain other countries do not believe in this system and are trying to destroy it in order to substitute one entirely different, where the individual is but one of many who are intended for service to the state. These principles are false, and we must counteract them.
To achieve these objectives, the Canadian citizenship branch is co-operating closely with the departments of education and national, provincial and local voluntary organizations, in the development of a citizenship program designed to assist in the adjustment of newcomers to the Canadian way of life, to stimulate the practice of our democratic principles, and to encourage in all citizens the will to accept their responsibilities as such.

Mr. Chairman, may I take the opportunity which this occasion offers to congratulate the minister on his appointment to the portfolio of citizenship and immigration.
All of us will have been impressed by the minister's concluding remarks respecting the work of the Canadian citizenship branch and the instructions that are given to those who are about to achieve citizenship, with a view -using the minister's words-to assuring a greater consciousness of the achievements of Canada in the past and also of the meaning of citizenship. With that aim and general purpose there will be unanimous agreement everywhere in the house.
The minister has mentioned the number of immigrants who have come to Canada in the last four years, and, as I remember the figure he gave, it was only some 20,000 under the
400,000	mark. Some came from other parts of the British commonwealth and others from the United States. Many came from continental Europe. A few years before the war there were many who felt that the migration to Canada of peoples from Europe might be detrimental to the building of a great Canadian citizenship, but if ever a viewpoint was dispelled the events between 1939 and 1945 gave an answer for all time. Those living in the prairie provinces are familiar with the large number of immigrants who came there during the period referred to by the minister, from 1900 until 1930, and saw something of the development that took place in western Canada in consequence of a dynamic immigration policy.


I like to mention the situation in my own province, and I like to think of the groups of people who came there from continental Europe. Many of them had been here only a few years at the time of the first great war, but large numbers enlisted. In the second great war I remember Major General La-Fleche referring on one occasion to the number of battalions of people of German, Ukrainian, Russian, Polish, Scandinavian and other origins who_ enlisted for overseas service in the Canadian army, a record noble and enduring. To read of those in my own constituency who won decorations in the last war, people with surnames indicating origins other than Anglo-Saxon or French, is to have presented an example of what our citizenship means and makes one realize that surname is not necessarily synonymous with citizenship.
I speak on this subject as one of mixed origin whose people came to this country 140 years ago, on my father's side to the province of Ontario and on my mother's side to the Selkirk settlement in 1812. From .the earliest days I advocated doing away with hyphenated citizenship in this country, whereby every ten years Canadians were required by the census regulations to declare their paternal origin, a requirement that was singularly annoying to those with non-Anglo-Saxon names who were thus denied the opportunity and privilege of being Canadians. Indeed our regulations were such that if the Duke of Windsor, an Englishman from the United Kingdom, had taken up residence in Alberta, every ten years he would have had to register by his German paternal origin. The continuance of such a practice would never permit the building of a strong Canadian consciousness.
When I first came to the house in 1940, and from then on, I pressed over and over again for the removal of regulations that denied to people the kind of citizenship we want in Canada. The minister speaks of Canadian unity. In my opinion nothing did more to give us a consciousness of our Canadian citizenship than the Canadian Citizenship Act of 1946. I have a certain pride in connection therewith. On the 11th of August, 1944, I advocated once more the removal of this requirement that was so detrimental to the building of Canadian citizenship, namely, the declaration of paternal origin every ten years. I recall that the then prime minister, Mr. King, stated that when the war was over he would join with me, and, as he said, with other hon. members of the same opinion, to achieve the kind of citizenship that all of us want to see developed in Canada. There is no question of denying

love of one's ancestry, but. a Canadian citizenship will never be built on the basis of looking back to the country of origin.
The Canadian Citizenship Act came into effect in 1946. My hon. friend says that anomalies have arisen since that time, and that they are to be removed, so far as may be practicable and possible, in the amendments that are to be introduced. I have one suggestion to make. It has to do with those who have come to this country from continental Europe. They came here because of our citizenship and the freedom that it implies. It is true that some who come to Canada may live here for ten, fifteen or twenty years without taking out citizenship, while reaping the advantages thereof, but the great majority of those who have come here from continental Europe since the war, realizing what this citizenship means, want to become citizens as soon as possible. They have to wait five years. Many of these displaced persons are stateless. For the first five years they are in Canada, they remain, as it were, set apart within our country. They ask for some recognition of their desire for citizenship.
I suggest to the minister that we give those people an opportunity to show their desire for this citizenship and all it means, by doing what is done in the United States-allow them to secure a certificate upon making a declaration of intention to take out citizenship at the end of two years. Such a certificate would be an indication of the newcomer's wish to be a Canadian citizen as soon as possible. It would be a token of his appreciation of what our system means, and what Canadian citizenship implies. It would be a popular move in Canada. Many hundreds and thousands would take advantage of it. It would not add to the cost of government. After all, in the scale of citizenship and its preservation, dollars do not weigh very heavily against the greater benefits that citizenship conveys. Give these people that opportunity. It would do a great deal to meet the attempt among non-English-speaking communities to undermine our country by the nefarious work of communism. It would set apart the holders of such certificates as prospective Canadians who were turning their back on communism and all for which it stands.
Two years ago the then secretary of state told us that there were 78 foreign language newspapers in Canada, of which no fewer than nineteen were preaching communism. I do not know what the figures are today, but that was the indictment of the then secretary of state, now Mr. Justice Gibson. Give those who want to be Canadians the opportunity

So long as that attitude prevails, so long as the idea is followed that we should not bring immigrants here unless we have jobs and houses waiting for them, it is my opinion that we will never have immigration to amount to anything.
I think the fallacy of these ideas is best demonstrated by the experience of the United States during the past century. In that country they had a tremendous flood of immigration particularly from the time of the civil war on, and people came in for many years at the rate of over a million a year. They did not come to jobs waiting for them; they did not come to houses waiting for them. They made jobs, they built houses, and in doing so created more and more employment for the people who were already there. In my opinion the same thing would happen in Canada if we would open the doors sufficiently wide to let people come in from Europe. In that regard I should like to put on the record part of an
[Mr. Harkness.l

article by Sir Norman Angell which appeared in the London Observer not long ago. It reads as follows:
One feature of the American experience vitally concerns the future of the British commonwealth. If we profit by its very plain lesson, the commonwealth may become, within the space of one lifetime, as great and as wealthy as is the United States today. But not if the lesson is rejected.
The year this writer was born (1874) the United States had a smaller population than Britain has today; and less than half the present combined population of Britain and the overseas dominions of Canada, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa.
At Lincoln's death the population of the United States, confederate and union states, negroes and whites combined, numbered little more than 30 million. It was a 30 million, moreover, inhabiting a country devastated by a murderous war, much of its best blood drained away in the enormous casualties, facing a bitter racial conflict still unresolved, and possessing (please note) a badly depreciated paper currency.
In other words, there was all the evidence at that time of what we would call a major depression and extremely bad conditions. The article continues:
Yet thousands bom into that situation were to live to see the 30-million nation become one of nearly 150 million, enjoying the highest standard of life for the common man anywhere in the world or at any period of history; and able, over and above that, out of its surplus, to furnish aid to half the world in its need.
While it is true that the factor of free immigration could not of itself, without political sagacity, have achieved for the United States today s result, it is also true that without free immigration no political wisdom would have sufficed. Consider the figures. In a little over the fifty years following the civil war the country admitted over 33 million immigrants; that is to say, a number in excess of the country's whole population at the beginning of that period. There were years-several-in which more than one million immigrants were admitted in the twelve months.
The world of the 19th century has also had its displaced persons problems . . .
I should like to continue reading a little further on in the article:
This immigration on a scale which in our day of quotas, restrictions, controls, planning, would be regarded as disastrous and impossible, did not disrupt the receiving country's economy; it greatly benefited thereby, since this alone made possible a rapid development of its natural resources.
It did not lower the American standard of life, which rose steadily all the time. It did not swamp the country's distinctive culture or political institutions_it was the means by which the effective
defence of those became possible. That unplanned world solved, without even knowing that it was doing it, and with great benefit to itself, a problem which our planned world finds in many of its aspects all but insoluble.
That is an example, Mr. Chairman, of what happened in the United States. If the same policy were followed here, similar results could be obtained. It is because of fear of the loss of their jobs, or competition from outside sources on the part of the various groups, that prevents the adoption of a policy

of at least partially free immigration. Until we get rid of that fear, which is based on completely fallacious reasoning as shown by what happened in the country to the south of us, we are not going to make great progress in this country. We are not going to have any appreciable amount of immigration.
I wish to mention, Mr. Chairman, some practical steps which could be taken to increase the amount of immigration. The difficulties which arise from the currency restrictions now in effect throughout the world have been mentioned. About two or three years ago the member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) and I were approached by some persons representing farmers of substantial means in the United Kingdom who wished to come to this country and bring out their capital in order to start farming. For the most part they were people engaged in the raising of purebred livestock of various types. They were people who could have made a great contribution to the purebred livestock industry in this country because they had the skills. We approached the then minister of immigration, as well as the minister of finance, in connection with the matter. They agreed it was desirable that these people be brought into the country. The scheme presented was that the dominion government would take over the assets of these people in the old country, and advance them funds in this country. Then as currency restrictions were removed, or as the opportunity arose, the government would dispose of these holdings in Great Britain, and thus recoup the money lent to these immigrants. There was no idea of making any gifts to these people, or anything like that. It was a matter of lending them the money, secured by assets in Great Britain. I could not see any reason why a scheme of that sort should not have been put into effect. It was a sound, practical scheme which would not have cost the dominion one cent because, in addition to the security the dominion had in the form of these assets in the old country, the government also had the land and livestock which the people purchased in this country. There was no possibility - of . losing, but nothing was done about it. The foreign exchange control board people said the scheme presented many difficulties, and, as I say, nothing came of it. I cite that as one example of something practical that could have been done to bring out some of the most desirable people as immigrants.
Another form which assistance to immigrants could take is that of a repayable loan to cover transportation expenses. I would be willing to admit that there might be some losses in that connection. A certain number

I should like to say a word or two now in connection with citizenship. The matter has been referred to in an excellent presentation by the member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefen-baker). I agree with him that the people of this country must get rid of this hyphenated Canadianism. I think that can be done best through the schools. As was pointed out by the member for Lake Centre, the people of the United States are not spoken of as German-Americans or Norwegian-Americans; they are all Americans. There is a unity of spirit which is patriotic, and which moves them. In Canada we have not got anything like the same spirit. A large number of people still look upon their country of origin with more affection than they regard Canada, the country to which they now belong.
I believe that one of the reasons for the great difference in this connection is that we have made no conscious effort to teach Canadianism to our school children. When I first went to school, it so happened that my family was in Denver, Colorado, for about nine months. I well remember that every day when we came into class the first thing we had to do was to salute the flag, which was up on the wall in front of us, and recite some sort of patriotic poem. Except for the recitation of the poem, this procedure was repeated every time we went into class; when we came in after recess; when we came in at noon; when we went out for afternoon recess; and when we left at four o'clock. The ceremony of saluting the flag impressed upon those small children the fact that they were Americans. It went on day after day. In addition to that, I remember there were a good many stories about the origin of the union, about the state of California and things of that sort. A strong and definite effort was made to teach Americanism to these children. My information is that the process continues right through public and high school. I think that is one of the main reasons why the people south of the border have succeeded in building up a spirit of nationhood and a spirit of unity amongst themselves so much better than we have. I believe we must follow their example if we are to accomplish the same results.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill from the Senate seeks to secure certain amendments to the charter of the United Grain Growers Limited of Winnipeg and Calgary. As a background to this measure, I should like to say that the company was first incorporated in 1906 under the Manitoba Joint Stock Companies Act. It was then known by the name of Manitoba Grain Growers Grain Company. In 1909 its original incorporation was replaced by a private act of the province of Manitoba. As its business developed along interprovincial lines it sought, and secured in 1911, a special dominion act of incorporation, which act was amended in 1918 to allow the company to distribute part of its earnings as patronage dividends.
In 1917 the company was merged with a similarly organized farmers' company in Alberta, known as the Alberta Farmers Co-operative Company, and the original act of incorporation changed the name of the amalgamated company to that of the United Grain Growers Limited. Other additional changes secured at that time provided that shareholders were to be grouped into locals for the purpose of appointing delegates to annual meetings, and proxy voting was disallowed. The original authorized capital of the company was $250,000. This was increased by the amendment of 1909 to $1 million, and upon federal incorporation in 1911 the capital authorized was further increased to $2 million, in $25 shares, limited in their sale to bona fide farmers, farmers' wives, renters of land, and with a limitation of 200 shares to any one person. A further increase in capital to $5 million was authorized at the time of the amalgamation with the Alberta company in 1917. The shares of the new company were exchanged for shares of the Alberta Farmers' Co-operative Company, and by 1930 the paid up capital stood at approximately $3,400,000.
In 1930 the company experienced some difficulty in replacing the shares of its members who had retired or passed away. It was their desire to keep their shareholder membership current and active. To meet this rather unusual situation the company, through a bylaw subsequently approved at an annual meeting, secured authority to divide its shares


into two classes. This authority allowed the company to issue 200,000 class "A" non-voting shares at a par value of $20, and 200,000 of class "B" membership shares at a par value of $5. These class "B" shares carried voting privileges of the delegates to the shareholders' annual meeting, but were not guaranteed as to dividends. Class "A" shares have a preference as to dividends to the extent of five per cent over any other payments or dividends that the company may make.
The total paid up capital of the company has remained at approximately $3,400,000 from 1930 to 1948. The company, however, has recently acquired a further line of 110 elevators in western Canada, and wishes to sell additional class "A" shares. There are at present 186,825 non-voting shares with a par value of $3,736,500, and 54,213 class "B" voting shares having a par value of $271,065. Briefly, that is the picture leading up to the present situation, so far as the company is concerned.
The main purpose of the amendments now proposed is to seek authority to do certain things that experience would appear to warrant. First of all, the company is seeking authority to increase its capital stock from $5 million to $7,500,000; second, to reduce the authorized number of class "B" voting shares from 200,000 to 100,000, and to convert these shares into class "A" shares. To date approximately 54,000 of these class "B" shares have been sold, and the directors feel that 100,000 will be sufficient to allow this type of shareholder to continue to control the company, particularly when the company has authority to purchase these shares for resale but is not allowed to retain more than ten per cent outstanding at any one time.
In section 8 of the bill, the company seeks powers granted ordinarily under the dominion Companies Act, and which are now generally granted as a matter of course to all companies seeking dominion incorporation, as well as similar powers being granted by most if not all provincial governments.
In section 9 of the bill it is seeking authority to bring the provisions with respect to payments of patronage dividends more in accordance with current practices.
The fifth rather important change has to do with company procedure as set out in section 10. The company holds a delegated annual meeting of shareholders once a year, and pays the expenses of all the delegates attending this annual meeting. This is usually a large item of expense. It frequently happens that at some of the meetings the directors secure authority in advance to do certain things. The company feels that

when such authority is granted at an annual meeting, it should not be required to place the same matter before a later annual meeting for endorsation.
The other amendments are largely for the purpose of clarification of the charter. I might add that the company has been in the grain business in western Canada for about 44 years. Its financial standing is sound, there having been only four years in the 1930's when it failed to meet its five per cent annual dividend. The original act of incorporation, together with the amending acts, discloses that the company conforms to the essential features of the Rochdale form of co-operative organization. It restricts the number of shares that may be owned by any one person, and adheres to the principle one share one vote. Since I took part in the debate on a similar bill the last time it was before the house I want to say a few words with respect to the present bill on this occasion. This is a proposed amendment to the labour code, which, as a statute of the federal parliament, applies to certain national industries in this country. I believe, Mr. Speaker-and I think this is an opinion that is held by a majority in this house and in the country-that the purpose of labour legislation is to provide an atmosphere in which management and labour can live and work together in a spirit of harmony, and with as little friction as possible, in order to make the industrial life of this country healthy and active.
When this same bill, and other proposed amendments to the labour code, were brought before the house on two previous occasions I took the stand, with other members, that it was too soon after the general revision of the labour code by this parliament seriously to consider amendments which were attacking certain basic principles of the whole legislation. A further time has passed and we may be coming to the stage when it will be necessary for this house and the government to examine the working of the labour code over the whole field, and to assess just how it is working out, and whether or not any changes-be they a part or be they a principle-should be made.
However, Mr. Speaker, I think it is still too soon to attempt to amend this general code in a way which does not agree with the basic principle of that act, and in that way undermine the basic principle without continuing to give a long searching look at the basic principle and deciding whether or not we want to continue to observe that principle.
I also think, Mr. Speaker, that when changes of this kind are suggested it would be advisable for the sponsors to give the house the benefit of a fairly searching review of the situation, to point out to the house just how they think experience has shown that a change of this nature is required, and why they think the particular change they suggest would contribute to the attainment of the basic purpose of labour legislation.
The hon. member who is sponsoring this bill has said that the subject matter has been supported by all the groups in this house, and he bases that statement, so far as the Liberal party is concerned, on the undoubted and firm purpose of that party to see that labour

Industrial Relations
unions in this country achieve the proper measure of security which will make it possible for them to carry out their proper function in our economic life. I disagree with him, however, when he suggests that that necessarily means that this party is in favour of the bill he has proposed. The basic principle of the national labour code, and the principle which, as I understand it, has guided the Liberal party in its approach to labour legislation, both in the past and at the present time, is that the function of labour legislation is to provide machinery whereby employees can organize and form themselves into a union, and whereby they will be given the opportunity and the right to bargain collectively with their employers and to reach an agreement with them, and protect themselves, by provision of legislation, from unfair labour practices and other things of that nature.
That is the basic principle, the basic purpose. But it is not regarded as advisable or wise to attempt by legislation to fix for employees or employers the conditions of labour, rates of pay or other matters of that kind which are regarded as proper subjects for negotiation between the parties. It is certainly my view that, in so far as these things are questions for negotiation between the parties, the soundest and safest situation for labour is to have them remain within their power as subjects for negotiation, as they see fit.
I do not think it would be in the interests of labour at the present time to impose by legislation the principle of this bill. A similar provision exists in labour codes of the various provinces, including my own. Provincial labour legislation has not, as a general rule, observed the same basic principle that has been the underlying principle of federal legislation. The situation in respect of industries and employers coming within the purview of federal legislation is in many cases quite different from that which applies to employers who come within the purview of provincial legislation.
This I regard as a very important question. It is one that should be considered carefully and given a great deal of study. I hope the house will consider it, and that the matter will be studied. If the new members in the house express themselves as being satisfied that these basic principles should be reconsidered, and the whole question gone into with this new approach in mind, then I think we should give consideration to that.
I am not prepared however to support amendment of our labour code in bits and pieces as is suggested by this bill. I therefore propose to vote against it.

The bill before us is one to amend the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, and has special reference to the voluntary revocable check-off. As one who has had some experience with open shop conditions in my own province prior to the bringing into force of legislation of this kind, I would have been prepared and willing to sponsor a bill of this kind. It had not occurred to me however that this provision was not almost Canada-wide. Perhaps this arises by virtue of the fact that in British Columbia we have such progressive legislation so far as labour and social provisions are concerned.
I do not intend to take up the time of the house to prove the great necessity for stable labour unions. They are the governing bodies of employees, and take the full responsibility for recommending legislation which will govern the working conditions, wages, holidays and other matters pertaining to labour. These unions must have some measure of security, and I would say that this bill calls for the very minimum of that which, in the usual normal term, could be considered the lowest form of union security.
National, provincial and municipal governments find certain expenditures necessary to carry out their various programs. Yet in many cases if it were not possible to have some measure of compulsion brought to bear to support those governing bodies it would be impossible and impracticable for them to carry on. Therefore it is not improper for us to assume that these labour unions, which are the responsible governing bodies, should also enjoy some measure of security. The one here sought is a very small measure indeed, and if it becomes law will tend toward greater harmony in labour and management relations.
I have in mind an organization in my own community which could not function if it were not for the check-off implemented in its behalf. I refer to the community chest. By the simple procedure of check-off the contributions are deducted by the employers, and as a result this community service is enabled to render invaluable support to each and every social problem developing in that area.

It would be unfortunate indeed if, when the community chest canvassers approached an employee, requesting him to sign one of their cards to support that worth-while project, they found that the union employee was unable to enjoy the same privilege in the matter of payment of union dues. He would therefore be prejudiced against assisting this worthy cause. He would quite correctly feel that here was a measure of discrimination. I have not heard a great deal of argument against this bill, but I had considerable discussion on the question before coming here and perhaps can envisage some of the objections.
One objection is that the government or the Department of Labour does not wish to interfere in labour-management relations. They assume that the two groups should come together on a bargaining basis free of every form of compulsion. However, if we review the act we find that there is a measure of compulsion in it. Once a union has gained certification the two parties must come together to reach an agreement. It is quite conceivable that having reached that position a union could force an employer to negotiate without compulsory legislation also. I do not think we should single out one item that will lend the union a small measure of security.
There is on the statute books other legislation which exercises a form of compulsion in what is commonly known as the free system of buying and selling. Labour has nothing but its labour to sell, but the farmer has his wheat, butter, eggs and so on to dispose of. On many occasions in the past there has been a measure of interference with free trade between the producer of farm products and the consumer. Only recently the price of wheat for the next crop year was set by the government of Canada. Most certainly a precedent has been set. I think this matter should come to a vote and I shall not take up any more time of the house.

From the rapid review which I have made of the development of trade unions in Canada, one will readily see that the greatest progress has taken place under the auspices of federal legislation in matters of labour relations. It was with the outbreak of the war that Canadian trade unions really went places, if I may use that expression. It was at a time when under the War Measures Act the central authority was vested with practically all jurisdiction in the field of labour legislation. During the war period and the two years immediately following, labour relations in Canada were regulated by the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, and also, after February, 1944, by the wartime labour relations regulations known as P.C. 1003. Since September, 1948,

roughly a year and a half ago, the present labour code, the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, has been the statute regulating labour relations in matters falling under the jurisdiction of the federal government.
The Industrial Disputes Investigation Act and P.C. 1003 provided valuable jurisprudence in matters of labour relations and acted as a model for the present labour code. As the house knows, the present labour code was not drafted, presented to the house and passed in a short time. It took over two years before all the processes which were followed were completed. Before the first draft was presented to the house in 1947 as Bill 338 the suggestions of all interested bodies and of the provincial governments were sought and taken into consideration for the purpose of improving the initial draft. Only after that first stage was the bill introduced and referred to the standing committee on labour relations during the session of 1947. In the course of the meetings of the committee written representations were received from a great number of responsible organizations across the country and several of them even sent representatives to appear before the committee. I need only refer to the Trades and Labour Congress, the Canadian Congress of Labour, the Canadian and Catholic Confederation of Labour, the Canadian Brotherhood of Railway Employees, the amalgamated unions, the Canadian Bar Association, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, the Canadian Construction Association. They presented their views and at the end of the session a report was made to the house that the committee should be reconvened in the following session, and that the same terms of reference be given to it.
In 1948, after having studied further written representations, the committee proceeded to examine the bill clause by clause and finally made a report recommending it to the consideration of the house. Therefore the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act has been given most careful study. Time, effort and consideration have been expended on it with the result that we now have a model act which has inspired most of the provincial legislation on similar matters.

Their keen sense of responsibility, their abounding courtesy, their personal kindness compel me to make this public acknowledgment. I assure you I do so with pleasure and without any reservation.
The international refugee organization cooperates, as far as Canada is concerned, with the Department of External Affairs, the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, the Department of Labour, and so forth. I want to concentrate on that phase of immigration for several reasons: First because I am convinced that many people are unaware of the great work, the important work, the humane work accomplished by the IRO in transporting refugees to Canada, to the United States and to other countries.
Then there is another reason. After the close of world war II, committees from various nations found themselves appalled by the.


serious condition of millions of displaced persons. Canada then played an important part -perhaps I may say a leading part-in urging the creation of a definite organization to handle the situation in some effective way. The United Kingdom and the United States were in complete agreement in pressing for what came to be known as IRO. Its constitution was signed by the Canadian government, and the Canadian parliament ratified the signature. Furthermore, the record shows that the resolution was adopted by a committee of united nations under the chairmanship of my good friend and fellow Canadian, Senator Turgeon of Vancouver. He also took a very active part in framing the constitution. It should also be kept in mind that the Canadian taxpayer is paying his share toward the financial upkeep of the IRO, and he is therefore entitled to know what is being done with his money.
These are some of the reasons why I deem it fitting to make known to the Canadian people, and to this parliament, the impressions I formed from actual observation of IRO activities.
I referred a minute ago to millions of displaced persons. During the war many of those people were forced to leave their homes, go into Germany and work as forced labour in German fields and factories. At the end of the war the allied armies liberated actually millions of them from concentration and labour camps in Germany. They were found to be from every country in Europe and represented almost every walk of life.
We are told that in the months immediately following the German surrender many highways in Europe were literally clogged with masses of refugees trekking back to their homes. By train, by truck and on foot, they wended their way back. What did they find when they got there? Those seven million people and more found their homes were no longer there. Their homes had been destroyed. Their livestock had been driven away; their farming implements were no more. They had the land, but nothing else. There they were like animals turned out into the fields to live or die. No doubt many of them in their despair would have preferred death. It was clear that something had to be done, and done quickly, if their lives were to be saved. I suggest that the practical efforts applied to the solution of that problem will go down in history as a lasting tribute to the Christian virtues of the United Nations.
But there was still another problem. Besides those seven or eight millions who had returned to their countries of origin there were another 1,600,000 refugees who

had to receive some other form of international assistance if their lives were to be saved. Many of them were still in Germany, some in Austria, some in Italy and other smaller countries. To re-establish those
1,600,000	was a hopeless task for any one nation to undertake. So, once again, United Nations got under the load.
Under the sponsorship of its general assembly a preparatory commission was set up which operated for over a year, until IRO could be constitutionally formed. This was completed on August 20, 1948. Under the terms of its constitution IRO became responsible-mark you, because responsible- for those 1,600,000 displaced persons, displaced from home and friends and thrown completely upon the charity of the allies.
Let me make it clear that there are seventeen countries who are members of IRO. Those countries pay the operating costs on an assessment basis. Canada's share is about $6 million per year. In other words IRO, although in a sense part and parcel of United Nations, is financed by the seventeen member countries, quite independent of United Nations funds. The head offices of IRO are in Geneva. That fact added to my interest in the organization, for during our two and a half weeks in Geneva I visited those offices several times. On each occasion I was profoundly impressed with the atmosphere of alertness, efficiency and sincerity that was everywhere manifest. The director general directs from the Geneva office an international staff of practically 2,500 persons, representing thirty-eight different nationalities, and assigned to twenty-six different countries. Among them are a good many Canadians, and those of them whom I met are mighty fine Canadians. I trust, Mr. Chairman, that I have now made fairly clear the creation of the IRO, as I found it, and that some idea of its work may be unfolded as I continue.
Hon. members will understand more clearly my interest in this question when I tell them that one of the highlights of our trip overseas was the greater part of an afternoon spent in a displaced persons camp during our days in Germany. We were in the city of Karlsruhe, where Canada has a most active branch office in the American zone. Karlsruhe, like many other cities through which we passed in Germany, carries the scars of war to a very marked degree. The IRO staff there is composed almost wholly of Canadians, and a more cordial, co-operative, efficient and friendly group it has never been my privilege to meet. We drove from Karlsruhe probably forty miles to this displaced persons camp, formerly a large German barracks, a formidable type of structure look-
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration ing well its part. It is what is called an assembly camp. It is recruited from some 58 or 60 minor camps quite a distance farther eastward. There I was able to grasp at first hand something of IRO activity, and still more of the responsibilities those officials were carrying.
On the day of our visit there were present 2,145 refugees, men, women and children, in the last stages of preparedness for transport across the Atlantic. A few were still being X-rayed, but the screening in general had been completed. One trainload was due to leave next day for Bremen, thence to New York, and another the following day to Montreal. I talked with several of the men, most of whom were Polish or Ukrainian, and some of whom could speak English. Reference to their homeland brought only a look of despair, but when one mentioned Canada their faces beamed.
I shall not take the time this evening to discuss immigration in general, because I may have an opportunity to do so later. May. I say I am quite in accord with some of the remarks made before six o'clock by the leader of the opposition. However, if some of those remarks were intended to apply to displaced persons camps-and I am not sure that they were-then I would have to say that those remarks were not all in accordance with the facts. I speak from my own personal observations. There are two or three points he made with which I would be compelled to take issue respectfully and perhaps reluctantly.
I would say that everything humanly possible is being done to make their stay over there comfortable, and their trip across the ocean pleasant. I confirmed that opinion by personal discussion with some of them on board ship during our return from the old land. Every effort is being made to take care of them there, to take care of them on the ship, and to see that they are carefully placed after they are landed. I am sure they appreciate it. I am very happy therefore that these people are assured of a friendly welcome upon arrival here. Why should they not be? Throughout Canada, and particularly in western Canada, those who came to us from European countries forty or fifty years ago proved valuable assets to this country. They entered upon manual labour of the hardest kind, very often such as was refused by our native-born Canadians. They took up land in rough, unsettled areas, thought by some to be valueless; but before long those crude surroundings reached the stage when "creaking wagons bore the harvest home and well-filled barns laughed with their golden plenty".

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
Today a great many of those farm homes are among the most desirable in western Canada. The sons and daughters are making progress in all branches of Canadian life, not only on the farms but in business, professional and public life as well. In fact, in the province of Manitoba there are five members, either of European birth or ancestry, in the provincial legislature. I have no hesitation in saying that Canada is a richer country today because of that immigration years ago; and it will be richer still as a result of this new flow of immigration coming to pur shores.
In one of the rooms we visited at the camp an elderly woman, intelligent and neat in appearance, was being instructed in languages by a younger one. It was explained to us that this woman was waiting and longing for the day when a certain technicality would have been overcome and she could join her friends in Canada. When about to leave I stepped across the room, shook hands with her and said as distinctly as I could, "I hope you will soon be in Canada". Whether it was the word "Canada" or just the little gesture of good will, I do not know, but the expression of gratitude shining through the tears that started coursing down that lonely woman's cheeks is something I shall not forget. Yes, an extra touch of kindness bestowed upon these people who come to us will make of them better Canadians and in a shorter time.
I can assure the committee that the afternoon spent in that camp was to us an enlightening and worth-while experience.
I wish very bluntly to ask my fellow Canadians, both in this chamber and outside it, this pointed question: If as a result of war in Canada you had lost your homes and all you had, everything taken over by an enemy, many of your loved ones gone, if you were compelled to seek refuge in a European country, compelled to begin life all over again in a land you had never known, under conditions you had never experienced, among people you had never seen, addressed in a language you had never heard, in your despair hoping for the bread of kindness, just what would your feelings be; what would be your reaction? Just think that over for a while. I suggest that with the war clouds not yet cleared away, this is no time for any of us to adopt a complex of superiority or selfishness. At present there are two of these assembly camps in the French zone, six in the American zone and four in the British zone.
I should like to mention some of the general features noticeable around those displaced persons' camps. Notwithstanding, the number transferred to other lands, there were


still living in or near those camps as of March 1, 1950, a total of 305,407 persons. They included 105,000 Poles, 42,000 Ukrainians and
19.000	Yugoslavs. You ask: How do those
305.000	people manage to live? Well, it is pretty tough. Let us realize that they are maintaining their morale today only by the hope of migrating soon to some other country to begin life all over again.
Those people of various nationalities, various cultures, various degrees of education, have learned to live together in harmony. Everywhere they are reported to be governing themselves along the democratic lines of the countries in which they wish to resettle. A number of them earn a scant living by taking up work of different kinds, some as farmers, some as road builders, some as professional men and some as artisans. Many of them are doing work far below their qualifications. The women appeared to be busy at knitting, sewing and embroidery, and apparently all are of a thrifty type. Educational facilities have been made available for both children and adults. Moving pictures of Canada are shown and informative discussions concerning Canada are held. Lectures are given on various topics, educational and otherwise, for there is no lack of experts in almost every field.
May I emphasize here that many of those displaced persons although lacking in financial assets are well educated and capable in other ways. It is stated that in Latvia and Estonia, the original homelands of many displaced persons, practically the same percentage of the population attended university as in Canada, and that in 1939 there was approximately the same number of students at the university of Riga as at the university of Toronto. No, they cannot be classed as an illiterate -people, not by any means.
From what I could see and learn I would suggest that now with the rush of immigration lessening to some extent the age of admissibility to Canada, now limited at 45 years, should be raised to age 50 at least. I would suggest also that the time has arrived when there should be more elasticity when one member of a family is found to be physically handicapped. To have a family barred from coming to Canada or broken up, to have some little one left behind in Europe, because it is not as strong as the others, seems to me rather harsh today, even if it were justified two or three years ago. Then again, permission for widows with one or more children, according to conditions, should be widened to the extent that each case be studied on its own merits.
I suggest this because I have confidence in the judgment of the men right on the ground

to make the proper selections. I have confidence in the screening, or security officers as they are called. I talked with two of them and could catch something of their difficulties. They have a tough job. They make every effort to be fair. It is not their wish to bar any worthy person nor do they want to admit the unworthy. Despite every precaution they will make an occasional mistake. That cannot be avoided. We are bound to get some misfits, but I ask whether there are any misfits among our own people.
We must also endeavour, so far as is reasonably possible, to keep down to a minimum that "hard core," as it is sometimes called, meaning the handicapped element. Norway has recently agreed to accept and care for one hundred of the blind among those unfortunates; Belgium 227 of the aged, now growing infirm; and Sweden 150 of those who

It is to the credit of Canada, and I say it with pride, that ours was the first country to accept displaced persons from overseas. We began with fifty-four, who sailed for Canada on the Aquitania on April 4, 1947, and since then Canada's record compares favourably with that of any other country. From that time there has been a total of 43,000 workers brought to Canada under the arrangements made by the interdepartmental immigration committee. This is the break-down:	for
domestic service approximately 10,400; for farms, 13,289; heavy labour, 19,000; and for nursing, interneship and professional service, 300. In addition to the 43,000 workers there were 3,388 wives or children of those workers who came along with them. In addition to those 46,388, there were over 55,000 wives and children of workers who had been left in d.p. camps and who were brought out after the workers became established. Some others were relatives or close connections of those already here. Canada has actually brought across 101,388 refugees to date. Here I should point out that Canada agreed in the first place to accept only five thousand displaced persons, but as you will note we have exceeded that number twenty times over.
There are those who say that because of our housing shortage immigration should not be encouraged. In that connection someone has made the apt remark that the greatest housing shortage this country has ever known was the day Jacques Cartier landed on the shores of Gaspe. Others claim we have all the population now we can assimilate. If I
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration remember correctly a somewhat similar claim was made long years ago by the Hudson's Bay Company. Those coming into western or northern Canada at that time to embark upon other activities were mostly regarded as aliens, intruding upon the supposedly sacred precincts of the fur industry. I take it we have far outgrown a mental attitude of that kind, particularly when we stop to consider that Canada's land area is greater even than that of the United States and Alaska, and comprises 28 per cent of the land area of the British commonwealth. Ever since the days when -the fur industry reigned supreme in western and northern Canada increased population and increased production have gone forward hand in hand in the development and the enrichment of Canada. Would any process of depopulation and decreased production spell any greater, or as great, prosperity for our people? The answer is obvious.
The IRO was supposed to discontinue operations on June 30 next, but it is pleasing to note that the time has been extended by United Nations up to March 31, 1951. After that date further arrangements will go into effect. I have taken longer than I would have wished in discussing the set-up and work of the IRO, but I feel that it is information to which Canadians are entitled, and which they will be glad to receive. I hope to have something to say at a later date on the subject of general immigration.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in conclusion may I point this out, that in the setting up of an organization to this end, in the adjusting of a thousand details and difficulties never even thought of by the general public, in the securing of an efficient and sympathetic personnel in many different centres, the fact of transportation congestion resulting from the huge number of returned men and women, who were so gladly brought back to Canada and re-absorbed into our economy, in placing those refugees at work when they arrived in Canada and in attaining the phenomenal results expressed in the figures I have just quoted, I am sure every thoughtful person will agree that the Department of Labour is entitled to sincere congratulations and the highest praise. A writer remarked not long ago that the achievement of bringing those refugees here in the face of the many difficulties that had to be overcome is as remarkable a performance as anything to be found in the history of immigration to Canada.
